title: Animals' rights
hookLine: don't overload, don't brand faces, don't make them targets (Muslim)

lines: A CAMEL IN A WALLED GARDEN.
cards: Tears, running from a camel's eyes. That's where a report in Abu Dawud begins, in a walled garden in Medina belonging to a man of the Ansar.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ steps inside, and the camel tied there sees him and begins to groan. He strokes it behind the ears until it settles, then asks: whose camel is this? A young man comes running.
And the Prophet tells him to fear God about this animal, because it has complained that its owner starves it and wears it out.

teach.b: Day two hundred seventy-two gave us the man who carried water up a well for a thirsty dog. Today, the law's side. The Qur'an sets the frame.
In surah six, every creature on the earth and every bird that flies on two wings are communities like you, and they too will be gathered to their Lord. Communities, not furniture.
From that the fiqh books draw duties, and today's three come from the hadith.

teach.h: DON'T OVERLOAD: FEED AND REST THEM.

teach.b: Another report in Abu Dawud tells of the Prophet passing a camel so thin its back had nearly reached its belly: fear God about these animals that cannot speak; ride them while they are fit, and eat of them while they are fit.
The jurists made it a rule: an owner must feed an animal and may not work it beyond its strength.

teach.h: DON'T BRAND OR STRIKE THE FACE.
teach.b: Second, don't brand or strike faces. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet forbids hitting the face and branding the face, and when he passes a donkey branded on its face, he curses whoever did it.

Third, don't make them targets. Also in Sahih Muslim, Ibn Umar comes across young men shooting at a bird they've tied up. They scatter, and he tells them the Prophet cursed anyone who makes a living thing a target.
So the fiqh books speak of an animal's rights the way they speak of a neighbor's: food, rest, a fair load, a face left unbranded. A camel can't file a complaint.
The tradition says it filed one anyway, and the Prophet heard it.

how: Islamic law requires owners to feed and rest their animals and not to overwork them, and forbids striking or branding their faces and using living creatures as targets.

o: what an animal is owed: food, rest, a fair load, no harm
a ban on eating meat, to spare every creature pain
laws that forbid Muslims from keeping animals as pets

p: the Prophet cursed whoever did it
stopped the young men shooting a bird

s: in Islamic law, animals are property with no rights of their own
the fiqh books list what an animal is owed: food, rest, a fair load.
the Prophet forbade branding an animal's face
the report is in Sahih Muslim, with the branded donkey.
shooting at a tied-up animal for sport is allowed if no one owns it
Ibn Umar reports the Prophet cursed anyone who makes a living thing a target.

games.q: you're Ibn Umar. you come across young men who have tied up a bird and are taking turns shooting at it. what do you do?
o: walk on; it's only a bird.
stop them and tell them the Prophet cursed whoever makes a living thing a target.
ask them to aim more carefully.
games.why: the young men scatter when they see Ibn Umar, and he repeats the Prophet's curse on anyone who uses a living thing as a target.

practice: If there's a pet near you, check its water and sit with it a while.

If not, bring to mind an animal you see often, a neighbor's dog, a bird on the wire, and ask what it needs that only a person can give: food, water, shade, a lighter load. Hold it kindly, and if you pray, you can remember it there.

wordCard.voice: Animals' rights. In Islamic law, what an animal is owed: food, rest, a fair load, a face left unharmed, and never to be used as a target. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a right, what is owed; also truth.

carryVoice: Your line: they have rights. Even the ones who can't speak for themselves. I'll be here tomorrow.
